Preparation and characterization of novel polyols-based DESs and their use in efficient sequestration of radioactive iodine
<::logo: Check for updates A square button with a gray background and a red bookmark icon inside a blue and yellow circle::>
Masooma Siddiqui ᵃ , Md Sayem Alam ᵇ , Maroof Ali ᵃ,*

a Department of Chemistry, Aligarh Muslim University, Aligarh, U.P. 202002, India b Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) - Central Leather Research Institute (CLRI), Polymer Science & Technology, Adyar, Chennai 600 020, India
ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Deep eutectic solvents Density Viscosity Iodine-capture Solvatochromism

ABSTRACT The utilization of Novel DESs can be greener alternative to traditional organic solvents. In present study, four polyols-based DESs are synthesized and characterized by several techniques. The prepared DESs are used for the efficient capture of hazardous iodine. In present study by simple combination of two readily accessible, economical, and biodegradable components four polyols-based DESs have been prepared. For the creation of these DESs, a hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) (polyols) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) (BTEAC) are used, which have melting points far lower than their respective melting points. The developed DESs were investigated for their physicochemical properties such as density, dynamic viscosity. Our results revealed distinct trends in these properties across different DES compositions, highlighting unique molecular interactions and solvation capabilities. The FTIR and NMR characterization study indicated considerable intermolecular interaction between the various component of the DES system. Further, Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters were determined using Nile red dye, and other solvatochromic dyes. For synthesized DESs, the solvatochromic parameters ENT, normalized polarity parameter, π*, polarity / polarizability; β, hydrogen-bond acceptor basicity and α, hydrogen-bond donor acidity, have been determined. The ENT parameters demonstrate that both non-specific and specific interactions play a significant role in solute-solvent interactions. The synthesized DESs have been utilized for the efficient capture of the iodine. The removal efficiency of DES depends upon the mass of the DESs taken and time duration. These findings deepen our understanding of DES behavior and underscore their versatility in diverse industrial and scientific applications.

## 1. Introduction Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are a new class of solvents those have gained significant attention in recent years due to their unique properties and potential applications [1,2]. DESs are formed by mixing two or more components, typically a hydrogen bond donor and a hydrogen bond acceptor, by forming hydrogen bonds in DESs governs their unique properties and functionality, influencing solvation behavior, solvent structure, and overall performance) [3,4]. which results in the formation of a eutectic mixture with a lower melting point than either of the individual components. This low melting point and the unique properties such as high thermal stability [5], low viscosity [6,7] and high solubility that make them attractive media for various applications [7]. They are non-toxic, biodegradable, and have low volatility, which makes them environmentally friendly. The properties of high melting point/viscosity/polarity of DESs can be further tuned by varying the components and

their ratios and render them suitable for various applications [8–10]. Over the past ten years, nuclear reactors have consistently supplied 10% or less of the world's energy. Nuclear energy is anticipated to become more significant since it is a reliable and low-carbon energy source. Safety issues, nevertheless, continue to hinder its functioning. The vol- atile radioactive waste generated during the reprocessing of spent nu- clear fuels—which essentially comprises radionuclides like ¹²⁹I and ¹³¹I in the form of molecular iodine (I₂), etc. [11,12]. This is one of the biggest safety concerns. For the efficient removal and storage of these radioactive elements, DESs play a novel role in this era of chemistry [13–18]. Because of their advantageous qualities, such as low cost, simple preparation, and environmentally safe starting materials, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted a lot of attention as prospective extracting agents in recent years. A significant area of worry is the rise in the amount of radioactive iodine and its isotopes in the environment. Iodine's involvement in metabolic processes and bio-magnification caused radioactive iodine to accumulate in both the human body and at every level of the food chain. It has become a frightening situation for scientists and researchers to collect and remove radioactive iodine from the environment because of the thyroid gland's direct involvement with iodine in the human body. Through exposure to contaminated air or water, it can build up in the thyroid gland of both humans and animals. This can raise the risk of leukemia, thyroid cancer, and metabolic abnormalities. Due to its unusually long half-life of 1.57 years, 129I is detrimental to the biosphere. While 131I has a relatively short half-life of 8.02 days, when it builds up in human thyroid tissue, it can raise the risk of thyroid cancer. It is clear from past experiences that radioactive iodine causes thyroid damage and may be carcinogenic when it builds up in the atmosphere as a result of any radioactive fallout. In this study, developed four novel DESs are used for I2 removal and storage [21,22]. Utilizing I2 in cyclohexane solutions and ultra-violet-visible (UV/vis) spectroscopy, the effectiveness of DESs at removing I2 was investigated. The capture of iodine by DESs involves the formation of a stable complex between the iodine molecule and the solvent components. In the present study, novel DESs have been pre-pared hydrogen acceptor species Benzyl triethyl ammonium chloride (BTEAC) and hydrogen bond donor species — e.g., Resorcinol (RES), Catechol (CH), Phenol (PH), Pyrogallol (PY), in the molar ratio of 1:2. This DES formulation aligns with Type I DES classification (The HBA can be a quaternary ammonium salt, while the HBD can be a range of compounds such as carboxylic acids, amides, or alcohols), known for its eutectic behavior and versatile applications. The synthesized DESs are characterized by several techniques such as NMR, FTIR, and the struc-ture of synthesized DES is confirmed with data FTIR and NMR spec-troscopy [23,24]. The viscosity and density of pure and modified mixtures also studied to give an understanding of possible interactions present in the system. Further solvatochromic parameters such as the hydrogen-bond acidity, hydrogen-bond basicity, and dipolarity/polar-izability of synthesized DES made of ammonium-based salts as hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) and phenolic compound as hydrogen bond do-nors (HBDs) were determined in this work [25]. It furnishes the mean-ingful insight how the polarity of the DES components was affected by the chemical structure of the DES components. This study lays the groundwork for future research into the enhancement and practical implementation of this good potential solvent technology [22,26–29]. The synthesized DESs have been used for the efficient used of hazardous I2. Overall, deep eutectic solvents are a fascinating and promising area of research that has the potential to revolutionize many different industries [30,31]. While there are still many challenges to be overcome, the unique properties of DES make them an exciting avenue for future innovation and discovery [26,32]. The future of deep eutectic applica-tions is promising [33–35] with potential uses in various industries and the potential to contribute to the advancement of sustainable and green technologies [21,36–41]. While DESs have shown promise in various industrial applications, their suitability for therapeutic use remains a topic of exploration. Understanding their biocompatibility, toxicity profile, and potential interactions is essential for evaluating their viability in therapeutic applications [42–44].

## 2. Experiment ### 2.1. Materials Benzyl triethyl ammonium chloride (98 %), resorcinol (99 %), catechol (99 %), pyrogallol (99 %), and phenol (99 %) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, USA, in the highest purity possible. Cyclohexane (98 %) and iodine (≥95 %) were purchased from Acros Organics, and all the materials were used without further purification [45,46].

2.2. Preparation of DESs DESs were synthesized by mixing benzyl triethyl ammonium chlo-ride (BTEAC) and phenolic compound (resorcinol, catechol, pyrogallol, and phenol) at a defined molar ratio (1:2) (Fig. 1). The continuous and stirring while heating to 80 °C for 1 h at air pressure result a stable homogeneous liquid. All of the prepared DESs were dried for up to three hours at 60 °C in a vacuum oven. The synthesized DESs were maintained in a desiccator and kept in sealed laboratory vials [47-49]. The composition of HBA and HBDs are shown in Table S1. The water content of the DES constituents was measured using a Metrohm 831 Karl Fischer coulometer that was taken into consideration during the preparation of each mixture. The water content for DES1, DES2, DES3 and DES4 are 2550, 1860, 2165, and 1540 ppm, respectively.

### 3. Methods #### 3.1. Solubility measurements To check whether DESs are hydrophobic or hydrophilic in nature solubility test have been performed with water, benzene, and cyclohexane solvents (Table S2) [50,51].

3.2. Density measurements The densities (ρ) of pure DESs and their mixtures with water (10%, 25%, and 50% water) were measured using a U-tube digital density meter (Laboratory Density Meter (model no: DMA 5000 M), Anton Paar GmbH) with a repeatability of 1.105 g/cm³ and 0.01 K, at atmospheric pressure. The observations were made at atmospheric pressure and a temperature range of 293–343 K with a temperature interval of 5 K. A built-in Peltier thermostat (PT-100) with an accuracy of ±0.01 K controlled the temperature measurement range (from 293 to 343 K). The density was determined with 1.4 × 10⁻⁶ g cm⁻³ as the standard deviation [52].

3.3. Viscosity measurements Using the Microviscometer (model number: LOVIS 2000 ΜΕ) Microviscometer Module, Anton Paar GmbH, the viscosity of pure DESs and their mixture was measured at a temperature range from 293.15 to 343.15 K with a temperature interval of 5 K. A built-in Peltier thermostat with a precision of 0.01 K was used to regulate the measuring temperature (which ranged from 293.15 to 343.15 K). A syringe was used to transfer the necessary amount of liquid (around 1 ml), taking extra care to avoid introducing bubbles into the tube to prevent errors in the measurements. In this range of viscosity values the diameter of the capillary was 1.59 mm, and the error for this capillary was 0.01 % [52].

### 3.4. Fourier–transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements FTIR spectra of pure compounds and DESs were recorded by Perkin Elmer FTIR (8000) spectrophotometer at 298.15 K. The range of the scan was from 4000 to 400 cm⁻¹ [53-56].
3.5. *NMR measurements* NMR spectra of DESs have been recorded by JNM-ECZL series FT NMR in chloroform D and DMSO-$d_6$ solvents at 25 °C [55,57,58].

3.6. _UV-vis spectroscopy and fluorescence-spectroscopy_ The UV-Vis spectra of the stock solution of iodine in cyclohexane and in DES were measured using a UV2550 ultraviolet spectrophotom- eter (Shimadzu, Japan). ### 4. Iodine capture experiment 100 mL of cyclohexane was mixed with 0.5 g of solid iodine to create the iodine cyclohexane solution. The mixture above was then agitated to confirm the complete dissolution of stable iodine in cyclohexane.

The bottom of the quartz cuvette was then filled with 3 mL of the sample solution and 0.5 g of DES (aside from to explore the impact of mass). It was also possible to measure the pure iodine-cyclohexane solution's absorbance. Data were gathered at the following intervals of time: 1 min, 5 min, 10 min, 0.5 h, 1 h, 1.5 h, 2 h, 3 h, 4 h, 5 h, 6 h, and 7 h [45]. (vide supra I2 capture and kinetic).

## 5. Result and discussion ### 5.1. Structural properties of DESs #### 5.1.1. NMR and FTIR The NMR investigation has been done for synthesized DESs (Fig. S2). The signal at δ = 9.00 ppm attributed to the proton attached to hydroxyl group, further signal at δ = 9.35, 9.11,9.09, and 8.96 observed due to the proton attached to H, N, O group in (Fig. S2) shows the interaction of BTEAC with polyols. Fig. 2(a) and (b) depict the FTIR spectra of a pure components and four synthesized DESs, respectively. The stretching vibration of polyols C—O was to the bands at 1220 cm⁻¹. The two

absorption peaks between 1450 and 1600 cm-1 are due to the C=C stretching vibration in the phenyl ring. While the peaks of OH groups in resorcinol and pyrogallol were close to 3250 cm-1 and the distinctive hydroxyl peaks in phenol and catechol were at 3400 cm-1. A sharp peak that was attributed to free hydroxyls seen in (Fig. 2(a)). A strong peak at 2950 cm-1 to 3000 cm-1 and towering peaks between 700 cm-1 and 790 cm-1 are characteristics of benzyl triethyl ammonium chloride (BTEAC). The four DESs' FTIR spectra differ significantly from one another (Fig. 2(b)). Because of the association of the hydroxyl group involving in hydrogen bonding, n(OH) in all DESs exhibited a broad peak at 3150 cm-1. This broadening of the peak hints about how chlo-rine molecules are involved in hydrogen bond formation. The creation of the N-Cl bond was also indicated by the change in FTIR frequency of three different oscillation modes, namely at v1, 3010 cm-1 to 3029 cm-1; v2, 1724 cm-1 to 1741 cm-1; and v3, 3156 cm-1 to 3124 cm-1. It shows after the formation of the DESs, the red shifts and broadening of the O-H and C-H stretching peaks can be attributed to the formation of hydrogen bonds between BTEAC and polyols.

Effect of water on viscosity The viscosity of DES is greatly influenced by the addition of cosolvent such as water, etc. Fig. 7. depicts the relationship between the DES's viscosity and the weight percentage of water in the DES. The viscosity of the DES decreases as the weight percentage of water in the solvent increases. This relationship exists because water has a low viscosity in comparison to the other components of the DES. If DES is to be used in a flow-through process, a lower viscosity may be preferred to facilitate solvent flow. It is possible to create a highly efficient deep eutectic solvent with a customized viscosity that satisfied the needs of particular application. Further, it is worthy to mention here, that addition of small amount of water to DES drastically decrease the viscosity of DES. On addition of 25 % of water, there is 100-fold decrease in viscosity. This behaviour of the viscosity of aqueous DES mixture may be due to large differences in the size and/or the shape of the component species of the mixture and the loss of Coulombic attractive interaction (or dipolar association) or rupture of H-bonding network within the mixture as compared to that in the neat components which result in sharp decrease in the viscosity. The viscosity data at different wt% of water is fitted by equation $\eta = \eta_0e-E\eta/RT$ and the recovered parameters have been given in Table 3.

The enhanced efficiency of radioactive iodine (I2) capture in synthesized deep eutectic solvent (DES) can be attributed to a specific mechanism involving the interplay of electrostatic and hydrogen bonding interactions. The presence of benzyl triethyl ammonium chloride in the DES introduces electrostatic attractions between chloride and ammonium ions, which are essential for solubilizing iodine molecules. However, the formation of hydrogen bonds within the DES matrix serves to weaken the electrostatic attraction between chloride and ammonium ions. This reduction in electrostatic forces allows for stronger interactions between chlorine and iodine molecules, facilitating more effective iodine removal. Consequently, the synergy between weakened electrostatic attractions and strengthened hydrogen bonding leads to improved efficiency in capturing radioactive iodine. ## 8. Conclusion The results of this study show that DESs are potential future materials for extensive industrial radioiodine removal. In this study, the preparation of four BTEAC-based DESs and the study of their physical properties such as water solubility, density, viscosity, and FTIR and ¹HNMR spectroscopic analysis shows the interaction of BTEAC and aromatic phenols show I₂. The ability of the deep eutectic solvent to capture iodine from hexane solutions was then tested. The outcomes demonstrated that the DESs were effective at capturing iodine. The maximum iodine uptake of 80 % at a solvent-to-iodine ratio of 1:2. Further was observed DES polarity HBD and HBA interaction and solvatochromism parameters are studied with fluorescence spectroscopy and UV-Vis spectroscopy with probes Nile red and coumarin. All these results give a conclusion that the more polar the DES is the less efficient for the removal of iodine, DES-4 is the most polar and least efficient for iodine removal, and follow the trend by DES-4 < DES-2-DES-1 < DES-3. The efficiency of I₂ capture could range from 85 % to 99 % along with the change of mass ratio of DES-3. Overall, the findings indicate that the deep eutectic solvent synthesized in this study has the potential to be a new material for iodine capture. The DESs have several advantages over other solvents and adsorbents, including low volatility, good thermal stability, and a high iodine uptake capacity [59]. However, additional research is required to optimize the solvent composition, assess its stability under different conditions, and evaluate its performance in real-world applications [26,28,29,41,64]. Finally, the successful synthesis and characterization of the deep eutectic solvent, as well as its effective application for iodine capture, represent a significant progression in the development of new materials for environmental remediation. Interest in DESs is rapidly growing due to their disruptive potential and diverse applications. Both startups and established corporations worldwide are increasingly recognizing the value of DES technology. Fostering innovation and collaboration is crucial for translating DES research into commercial products. By supporting entrepreneurial efforts and technology transfer, we can speed up DES adoption. Scalability is key, as practical use depends on cost-effective, large-scale production. While initial experiments show DESs' effectiveness in iodine capture, achieving commercial potential requires scalable manufacturing, optimized production, and economic feasibility. Moreover, our exploration of DES applications extends far beyond iodine capture, encompassing a diverse array of industries and scientific disciplines [27,32,33].

Below the drawing, the word "ELSEVIER" is written in a sans-serif font.::> Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Journal of Molecular Liquids journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/molliq <::logo: Elsevier journal of MOLECULAR LIQUIDS A gold and purple journal cover with a small 'PPL' logo in the top left corner.::> Preparation and characterization of novel polyols-based DESs and their use in efficient sequestration of radioactive iodine <::logo: Check for updates A square button with a gray background and a red bookmark icon inside a blue and yellow circle::> Masooma Siddiqui ᵃ , Md Sayem Alam ᵇ , Maroof Ali ᵃ,* a Department of Chemistry, Aligarh Muslim University, Aligarh, U.P. 202002, India b Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) - Central Leather Research Institute (CLRI), Polymer Science & Technology, Adyar, Chennai 600 020, India ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Deep eutectic solvents Density Viscosity Iodine-capture Solvatochromism ABSTRACT The utilization of Novel DESs can be greener alternative to traditional organic solvents. In present study, four polyols-based DESs are synthesized and characterized by several techniques. The prepared DESs are used for the efficient capture of hazardous iodine. In present study by simple combination of two readily accessible, economical, and biodegradable components four polyols-based DESs have been prepared. For the creation of these DESs, a hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) (polyols) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) (BTEAC) are used, which have melting points far lower than their respective melting points. The developed DESs were investigated for their physicochemical properties such as density, dynamic viscosity. Our results revealed distinct trends in these properties across different DES compositions, highlighting unique molecular interactions and solvation capabilities. The FTIR and NMR characterization study indicated considerable intermolecular interaction between the various component of the DES system. Further, Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters were determined using Nile red dye, and other solvatochromic dyes. For synthesized DESs, the solvatochromic parameters ENT, normalized polarity parameter, π*, polarity / polarizability; β, hydrogen-bond acceptor basicity and α, hydrogen-bond donor acidity, have been determined. The ENT parameters demonstrate that both non-specific and specific interactions play a significant role in solute-solvent interactions. The synthesized DESs have been utilized for the efficient capture of the iodine. The removal efficiency of DES depends upon the mass of the DESs taken and time duration. These findings deepen our understanding of DES behavior and underscore their versatility in diverse industrial and scientific applications. ## 1. Introduction Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are a new class of solvents those have gained significant attention in recent years due to their unique properties and potential applications [1,2]. DESs are formed by mixing two or more components, typically a hydrogen bond donor and a hydrogen bond acceptor, by forming hydrogen bonds in DESs governs their unique properties and functionality, influencing solvation behavior, solvent structure, and overall performance) [3,4]. which results in the formation of a eutectic mixture with a lower melting point than either of the individual components. This low melting point and the unique properties such as high thermal stability [5], low viscosity [6,7] and high solubility that make them attractive media for various applications [7]. They are non-toxic, biodegradable, and have low volatility, which makes them environmentally friendly. The properties of high melting point/viscosity/polarity of DESs can be further tuned by varying the components and their ratios and render them suitable for various applications [8–10]. Over the past ten years, nuclear reactors have consistently supplied 10% or less of the world's energy. Nuclear energy is anticipated to become more significant since it is a reliable and low-carbon energy source. Safety issues, nevertheless, continue to hinder its functioning. The vol- atile radioactive waste generated during the reprocessing of spent nu- clear fuels—which essentially comprises radionuclides like ¹²⁹I and ¹³¹I in the form of molecular iodine (I₂), etc. [11,12]. This is one of the biggest safety concerns. For the efficient removal and storage of these radioactive elements, DESs play a novel role in this era of chemistry [13–18]. Because of their advantageous qualities, such as low cost, simple preparation, and environmentally safe starting materials, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted a lot of attention as prospective extracting agents in recent years. Iodine excess is becoming more com- mon, raising worries about the risks associated with it, including hy- pothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, malignancies, autoimmune thyroid --- * Corresponding author. Today, it is understood that iodine excess poses a risk to both human and animal development [20]. A significant area of worry is the rise in the amount of radioactive iodine and its isotopes in the environment. Iodine's involvement in metabolic processes and bio-magnification caused radioactive iodine to accumulate in both the human body and at every level of the food chain. It has become a frightening situation for scientists and researchers to collect and remove radioactive iodine from the environment because of the thyroid gland's direct involvement with iodine in the human body. Through exposure to contaminated air or water, it can build up in the thyroid gland of both humans and animals. This can raise the risk of leukemia, thyroid cancer, and metabolic abnormalities. Due to its unusually long half-life of 1.57 years, 129I is detrimental to the biosphere. While 131I has a relatively short half-life of 8.02 days, when it builds up in human thyroid tissue, it can raise the risk of thyroid cancer. It is clear from past experiences that radioactive iodine causes thyroid damage and may be carcinogenic when it builds up in the atmosphere as a result of any radioactive fallout. In this study, developed four novel DESs are used for I2 removal and storage [21,22]. Utilizing I2 in cyclohexane solutions and ultra-violet-visible (UV/vis) spectroscopy, the effectiveness of DESs at removing I2 was investigated. The capture of iodine by DESs involves the formation of a stable complex between the iodine molecule and the solvent components. In the present study, novel DESs have been pre-pared hydrogen acceptor species Benzyl triethyl ammonium chloride (BTEAC) and hydrogen bond donor species — e.g., Resorcinol (RES), Catechol (CH), Phenol (PH), Pyrogallol (PY), in the molar ratio of 1:2. This DES formulation aligns with Type I DES classification (The HBA can be a quaternary ammonium salt, while the HBD can be a range of compounds such as carboxylic acids, amides, or alcohols), known for its eutectic behavior and versatile applications. The synthesized DESs are characterized by several techniques such as NMR, FTIR, and the struc-ture of synthesized DES is confirmed with data FTIR and NMR spec-troscopy [23,24]. The viscosity and density of pure and modified mixtures also studied to give an understanding of possible interactions present in the system. Further solvatochromic parameters such as the hydrogen-bond acidity, hydrogen-bond basicity, and dipolarity/polar-izability of synthesized DES made of ammonium-based salts as hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) and phenolic compound as hydrogen bond do-nors (HBDs) were determined in this work [25]. It furnishes the mean-ingful insight how the polarity of the DES components was affected by the chemical structure of the DES components. This study lays the groundwork for future research into the enhancement and practical implementation of this good potential solvent technology [22,26–29]. The synthesized DESs have been used for the efficient used of hazardous I2. Overall, deep eutectic solvents are a fascinating and promising area of research that has the potential to revolutionize many different industries [30,31]. While there are still many challenges to be overcome, the unique properties of DES make them an exciting avenue for future innovation and discovery [26,32]. The future of deep eutectic applica-tions is promising [33–35] with potential uses in various industries and the potential to contribute to the advancement of sustainable and green technologies [21,36–41]. While DESs have shown promise in various industrial applications, their suitability for therapeutic use remains a topic of exploration. Understanding their biocompatibility, toxicity profile, and potential interactions is essential for evaluating their viability in therapeutic applications [42–44]. ## 2. Experiment ### 2.1. Materials Benzyl triethyl ammonium chloride (98 %), resorcinol (99 %), catechol (99 %), pyrogallol (99 %), and phenol (99 %) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, USA, in the highest purity possible. Cyclohexane (98 %) and iodine (≥95 %) were purchased from Acros Organics, and all the materials were used without further purification [45,46]. 2.2. Preparation of DESs DESs were synthesized by mixing benzyl triethyl ammonium chlo-ride (BTEAC) and phenolic compound (resorcinol, catechol, pyrogallol, and phenol) at a defined molar ratio (1:2) (Fig. 1). The continuous and stirring while heating to 80 °C for 1 h at air pressure result a stable homogeneous liquid. All of the prepared DESs were dried for up to three hours at 60 °C in a vacuum oven. The synthesized DESs were maintained in a desiccator and kept in sealed laboratory vials [47-49]. The composition of HBA and HBDs are shown in Table S1. The water content of the DES constituents was measured using a Metrohm 831 Karl Fischer coulometer that was taken into consideration during the preparation of each mixture. The water content for DES1, DES2, DES3 and DES4 are 2550, 1860, 2165, and 1540 ppm, respectively. ### 3. Methods #### 3.1. Solubility measurements To check whether DESs are hydrophobic or hydrophilic in nature solubility test have been performed with water, benzene, and cyclohexane solvents (Table S2) [50,51]. 3.2. Density measurements The densities (ρ) of pure DESs and their mixtures with water (10%, 25%, and 50% water) were measured using a U-tube digital density meter (Laboratory Density Meter (model no: DMA 5000 M), Anton Paar GmbH) with a repeatability of 1.105 g/cm³ and 0.01 K, at atmospheric pressure. The observations were made at atmospheric pressure and a temperature range of 293–343 K with a temperature interval of 5 K. A built-in Peltier thermostat (PT-100) with an accuracy of ±0.01 K controlled the temperature measurement range (from 293 to 343 K). The density was determined with 1.4 × 10⁻⁶ g cm⁻³ as the standard deviation [52]. 3.3. Viscosity measurements Using the Microviscometer (model number: LOVIS 2000 ΜΕ) Microviscometer Module, Anton Paar GmbH, the viscosity of pure DESs and their mixture was measured at a temperature range from 293.15 to 343.15 K with a temperature interval of 5 K. A built-in Peltier thermostat with a precision of 0.01 K was used to regulate the measuring temperature (which ranged from 293.15 to 343.15 K). A syringe was used to transfer the necessary amount of liquid (around 1 ml), taking extra care to avoid introducing bubbles into the tube to prevent errors in the measurements. In this range of viscosity values the diameter of the capillary was 1.59 mm, and the error for this capillary was 0.01 % [52]. ### 3.4. Fourier–transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements FTIR spectra of pure compounds and DESs were recorded by Perkin Elmer FTIR (8000) spectrophotometer at 298.15 K. The range of the scan was from 4000 to 400 cm⁻¹ [53-56]. 3.5. *NMR measurements* NMR spectra of DESs have been recorded by JNM-ECZL series FT NMR in chloroform D and DMSO-$d_6$ solvents at 25 °C [55,57,58]. 3.6. _UV-vis spectroscopy and fluorescence-spectroscopy_ The UV-Vis spectra of the stock solution of iodine in cyclohexane and in DES were measured using a UV2550 ultraviolet spectrophotom- eter (Shimadzu, Japan). Conclusion The results of this study show that DESs are potential future materials for extensive industrial radioiodine removal. In this study, the preparation of four BTEAC-based DESs and the study of their physical properties such as water solubility, density, viscosity, and FTIR and ¹HNMR spectroscopic analysis shows the interaction of BTEAC and aromatic phenols show I₂. The ability of the deep eutectic solvent to capture iodine from hexane solutions was then tested. The outcomes demonstrated that the DESs were effective at capturing iodine. The maximum iodine uptake of 80 % at a solvent-to-iodine ratio of 1:2. Further was observed DES polarity HBD and HBA interaction and solvatochromism parameters are studied with fluorescence spectroscopy and UV-Vis spectroscopy with probes Nile red and coumarin. All these results give a conclusion that the more polar the DES is the less efficient for the removal of iodine, DES-4 is the most polar and least efficient for iodine removal, and follow the trend by DES-4 < DES-2-DES-1 < DES-3. The efficiency of I₂ capture could range from 85 % to 99 % along with the change of mass ratio of DES-3. Overall, the findings indicate that the deep eutectic solvent synthesized in this study has the potential to be a new material for iodine capture. The DESs have several advantages over other solvents and adsorbents, including low volatility, good thermal stability, and a high iodine uptake capacity [59]. However, additional research is required to optimize the solvent composition, assess its stability under different conditions, and evaluate its performance in real-world applications [26,28,29,41,64]. Finally, the successful synthesis and characterization of the deep eutectic solvent, as well as its effective application for iodine capture, represent a significant progression in the development of new materials for environmental remediation. Interest in DESs is rapidly growing due to their disruptive potential and diverse applications. Both startups and established corporations worldwide are increasingly recognizing the value of DES technology. Fostering innovation and collaboration is crucial for translating DES research into commercial products. By supporting entrepreneurial efforts and technology transfer, we can speed up DES adoption. Scalability is key, as practical use depends on cost-effective, large-scale production. While initial experiments show DESs' effectiveness in iodine capture, achieving commercial potential requires scalable manufacturing, optimized production, and economic feasibility. Moreover, our exploration of DES applications extends far beyond iodine capture, encompassing a diverse array of industries and scientific disciplines [27,32,33]. Conclusion The results of this study show that DESs are potential future materials for extensive industrial radioiodine removal. In this study, the preparation of four BTEAC-based DESs and the study of their physical properties such as water solubility, density, viscosity, and FTIR and ¹HNMR spectroscopic analysis shows the interaction of BTEAC and aromatic phenols show I₂. The ability of the deep eutectic solvent to capture iodine from hexane solutions was then tested. The outcomes demonstrated that the DESs were effective at capturing iodine. The maximum iodine uptake of 80 % at a solvent-to-iodine ratio of 1:2. Further was observed DES polarity HBD and HBA interaction and solvatochromism parameters are studied with fluorescence spectroscopy and UV-Vis spectroscopy with probes Nile red and coumarin. All these results give a conclusion that the more polar the DES is the less efficient for the removal of iodine, DES-4 is the most polar and least efficient for iodine removal, and follow the trend by DES-4 < DES-2-DES-1 < DES-3. The efficiency of I₂ capture could range from 85 % to 99 % along with the change of mass ratio of DES-3. Overall, the findings indicate that the deep eutectic solvent synthesized in this study has the potential to be a new material for iodine capture. The DESs have several advantages over other solvents and adsorbents, including low volatility, good thermal stability, and a high iodine uptake capacity [59]. However, additional research is required to optimize the solvent composition, assess its stability under different conditions, and evaluate its performance in real-world applications [26,28,29,41,64]. Finally, the successful synthesis and characterization of the deep eutectic solvent, as well as its effective application for iodine capture, represent a significant progression in the development of new materials for environmental remediation. Interest in DESs is rapidly growing due to their disruptive potential and diverse applications. Both startups and established corporations worldwide are increasingly recognizing the value of DES technology. Fostering innovation and collaboration is crucial for translating DES research into commercial products. By supporting entrepreneurial efforts and technology transfer, we can speed up DES adoption. Scalability is key, as practical use depends on cost-effective, large-scale production. While initial experiments show DESs' effectiveness in iodine capture, achieving commercial potential requires scalable manufacturing, optimized production, and economic feasibility. Moreover, our exploration of DES applications extends far beyond iodine capture, encompassing a diverse array of industries and scientific disciplines [27,32,33].
